21.quote_or_event: “Obeisance to all the Saints in the world.” … “This five-fold obeisance is destructive of all sins and is the foremost amongst all the auspicious.”
21.explanation: The Namokar (Navkar) Mantra, the first formula every Jain learns and the opening of the Saman Suttam anthology, ends its five salutations by bowing to every renunciant in the world, and the verse that follows declares this homage the foremost of all auspicious things.
21.tie_back: Where the Kural says the settled verdict of all worthy books is to praise renunciants above every other excellence, Jainism's own first and most-recited formula makes reverence for the world's renunciants, alongside the Jinas, the highest auspicious act.
21.source: Namokar Mantra as Saman Suttam vv. 1-2, Mangalasutra (tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; text via jainworld.com)
21._accuracy_note: A strong, distinctly Jain match for honouring renunciants above all, though the mantra salutes five classes of perfected and practising souls rather than ascetics alone; the jainworld page prints 'inthe', silently corrected to 'in the'.

22.quote_or_event: “‘All sounds recoil thence, where speculation has no room,’ nor does the mind penetrate there.” … “he perceives, he knows, but there is no analogy (whereby to know the nature of the liberated soul).”
22.explanation: At the close of its fifth lecture the Acaranga Sutra describes the state of the one who has left the round of birth and death, and says that words, reasoning and even comparison cannot reach or measure it.
22.tie_back: The Kural says that trying to put a measure on the greatness of renunciants is like counting all the dead, a category error rather than a hard sum; the Acaranga likewise says the renouncer's final state has no measure in words or analogy.
22.source: Acaranga Sutra I.5.6.3-4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
22._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts, but the Acaranga speaks of the liberated soul (siddha) rather than the living ascetic, and of inexpressibility rather than numberlessness, so the fit is thematic and partial.

23.quote_or_event: “He who, in the world, comprehends and renounces these causes of sin, is called a reward-knowing sage (muni).”
23.explanation: The very first lesson of the Acaranga Sutra sets out the twofold knowledge (parijna): first understanding the causes of sin and rebirth, then renouncing them. Only the person who does both is called a true sage (muni).
23.tie_back: Valluvar's renunciant first discerns the two orders of existence ('vakai therindhu') and then takes up virtue here and now. That is the same two-step the Acaranga sets at the head of the Jain canon, where comprehension has to pass into renunciation in this life.
23.source: Acaranga Sutra I.1.1.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
23._accuracy_note: Close structural match to discern-then-adopt, especially under the birth-versus-release reading of 'irumai', though the Acaranga does not itself speak of 'two' things or of the renouncer's greatness shining in the world.

24.quote_or_event: “Having heard these well-spoken words of the virtuous lady, he returned to the Law like an elephant driven by the hook. Protected in thoughts, words, and acts, subduing his senses and keeping the vows, he practised true Sramanahood throughout life.”
24.explanation: The monk Rathanemi, overcome by desire on seeing the nun Rajimati, is brought back by her firm rebuke as a mahout's hook brings back an elephant. He then masters his senses, and the lecture says both of them became omniscient (kevalins) and reached perfection.
24.tie_back: This is the Kural's own image almost word for word: the goad (thotti, the ankusa) of firm resolve turns the elephant of the senses back, and the person so controlled becomes the seed of the highest estate, which in this story ends in liberation.
24.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.46-48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895); vv. 42-46 recur in Dasavaikalika Sutra 2
24._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (diacritics simplified in 'Sramanahood'); the elephant-and-goad image and sense-control leading to perfection match closely, though in the story the goad is another person's words rather than the ascetic's own inner firmness.

25.quote_or_event: “Throwing off the guise of a Brahmana, and making visible his true form, Sakra saluted him respectfully and praised him with these sweet words” … “Here (on earth) you are the highest man, Reverend sir, and hereafter you will be the highest”
25.explanation: When King Nami renounces his throne, Sakra (Indra), king of the gods, comes disguised as a Brahmin to test him with arguments for worldly duty. When Nami's resolve holds, Indra shows his true form, praises Nami for having conquered anger, pride, delusion and greed, and circles him in reverence.
25.tie_back: The Kural names Indra as the witness to the power of the one who has quenched the five senses. In the Uttaradhyayana Indra literally takes that role, first testing the renouncer and then publicly testifying to his supremacy.
25.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.6-58, esp. 9.55-59 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
25._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (diacritics simplified) and a near one-to-one match; in Jain cosmology Indra is a karma-bound celestial, not a creator, which suits the Kural's use of him as witness, though the Ahalya allusion some commentators find has no Jain counterpart here.

26.quote_or_event: “As it is difficult to cross the heavenly Ganges, or to swim against the current, or to swim with one's arms over the sea, so it is difficult to get over the ocean of duties.” … ‘but in this world nothing is difficult for one who is free from desire.’
26.explanation: Mrigaputra's parents list at length how hard a monk's life is, from lifelong non-injury to swallowing 'iron grains', to talk him out of it. He answers that for one free of desire nothing is too hard, then takes the vows and reaches perfection.
26.tie_back: The Kural defines the great as those who do what is hard to do. The Uttaradhyayana spells out exactly how hard renunciation is, then shows a great soul doing it anyway.
26.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 19.24-44, esp. 19.36 and 19.44 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
26._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong thematic fit chosen to avoid the self-conquest motif already used in the Buddhism slot, though the Jain text does not draw the Kural's explicit great/small contrast.

27.quote_or_event: “The five senses, anger, pride, delusion, and greed--difficult to conquer is one's self; but when that is conquered, everything is conquered.”
27.explanation: Answering Indra's challenge to go out and conquer rival kings, the royal sage Nami says that the real enemies are the five senses and the passions, and that whoever masters them has mastered everything.
27.tie_back: The Kural says the world is in the grip of the one who fully understands the five, taste, sight, touch, sound and smell. Nami says the same thing: once the five senses are conquered, everything is conquered.
27._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match for mastery of the five bringing mastery of all, though the Jain verse adds the four passions and speaks of conquest rather than the Kural's discernment of sense-objects.

28.quote_or_event: “That alone is true Scripture which is the word of a Tirthamkara, which cannot be over-ridden in disputation, nor falsified by perception, reason or testimony, which reveals the nature of things, which is helpful to men, animals and all other kinds of beings, and which is potent enough to destroy all forms of falsehood.”
28.explanation: Samantabhadra grounds the authority of Jain scripture in the person who spoke it. A Tirthankara, free of every fault and omniscient, utters words that cannot be refuted and that benefit every living being.
28.tie_back: The Kural says the sacred sayings left on earth by people of perfected speech show their greatness. Jain tradition makes the same tie between the perfected person and the sacred word, though it argues from the speaker to the scripture rather than from the scripture back to the speaker.
28.source: Ratnakaranda Shravakachara v. 9 (tr. Champat Rai Jain, The Householder's Dharma, 1917)
28._accuracy_note: Verified against the archive.org scan (OCR 'Ttrihaijikara' read as 'Tirthamkara'); a good fit on the sage-and-sacred-word link, but the argument runs in the opposite direction to the Kural's, and Champat Rai's word 'God' for the apta in nearby verses means a perfected teacher, not a creator.

29.quote_or_event: ‘do not injure him who cannot be injured, lest he consume you all by the fire (of his virtue).’ … ‘for in his wrath he might reduce the world to ashes.’ … “There is not the least hatred in me, neither now, nor before, nor in future.”
29.explanation: When Brahmin youths beat the outcaste-born monk Harikesa, the lady Bhadra warns them that such an ascetic's power could burn the world, and his attendant Yakshas strike the attackers down. The monk himself then says he bears no hatred at all.
29.tie_back: Like the Kural, the story warns that whoever provokes one who stands on the hill of virtue cannot be shielded even for a moment. Jainism, though, takes the anger away from the monk: the danger lies in his power and in his divine protectors, while he himself stays free of wrath.
29.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 12.19-33, esp. 12.23, 12.28, 12.32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
29._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong narrative fit on the peril of offending an ascetic, but Jain doctrine treats anger (krodha) as a passion a true monk must not have, so it moves the retaliation away from the sage himself, a real difference from the Kural's 'veguli'.

30.quote_or_event: “He who thoroughly knows living beings, whether they move or not, and does not injure them in any of the three ways, him we call a Brahmana.” … “By one's actions one becomes a Brahmana, or a Kshattriya, or a Vaisya, or a Sudra.”
30.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha tells a sacrificing priest that a true Brahmin is defined not by birth or ritual but by conduct, above all by not harming any living being, moving or unmoving, in thought, word or deed.
30.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's redefinition of 'anthanar' by unbroken kindness toward every living thing. The Jain text is even more explicit that the title belongs to non-injury, which reaches to beings that do not move, rather than to birth.
30.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.19-33, esp. 25.23 and 25.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
30._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (diacritics simplified); a near one-to-one match on redefining the Brahmin by compassion for all beings, parallel to but independent of the Buddhist Brahmanavagga used in that slot.
